editorNote: Portable computing faces its first great after-sale test while modems bring both play and peril into the home.
morningLine: This week: Xerox steps behind stranded Osborne owners, a battery portable promises ten hours, and computer games gain an auteur-minded publisher.

lead.headline: Xerox Service Lifeline Reaches Osborne Owners
lead.dek: A fallen portable pioneer turns to an industry giant to keep its machines working.
body: Osborne Computer Corporation, once the most visible name in portable computing, announced October 11 that Xerox would service Osborne products while the manufacturer operated under federal bankruptcy protection. The pact offers owners a measure of continuity after the company’s swift reversal left the future of its machines and support network uncertain.

For customers, service is more than a footnote. Portable machines travel, absorb wear, and combine a display, disk drives, keyboard, and power supply in a tightly packed case. Access to Xerox’s established service organization may keep working Osborne systems productive even as the company that sold them reorganizes.

The arrangement also marks a sobering turn in the young personal-computer trade. Osborne helped prove that a complete computer could be carried from office to office, but rapid competition and financial distress showed that inventive hardware alone could not guarantee a stable supplier.

Xerox enters the story from both directions this week: it is supporting the installed Osborne base while introducing a portable machine of its own. Buyers now have a new question for every dazzling specification sheet—who will stand behind the computer after the sale?

stories.headline: Xerox Sunrise Claims a Ten-Hour Workday
stories.dek: The 1810 pairs 64,000 characters of memory with rechargeable batteries.
body: Xerox introduced its 1810 Sunrise portable in coverage dated October 13, describing a battery-powered machine with 64,000 characters of memory. The company said its rechargeable batteries could operate for ten hours, a striking claim in a field where “portable” often still means a heavy computer tied to a wall socket.

The announcement puts endurance at the center of mobility. If the claimed running time holds in daily use, the Sunrise points toward computers that can accompany a full working day instead of merely moving between outlets.

stories.headline: FBI Raids Bring Modem Intrusion Home
stories.dek: Seized home computers put teenage electronic trespass in the national spotlight.
body: Federal agents seized the home computers of four Irvine, California high-school students on October 13 as part of a multistate inquiry into suspected electronic intrusion. A follow-up report described a nationwide wire-fraud investigation involving alleged entry into defense and payroll systems.

The reports give the home modem a new and uneasy prominence. The same communications links that let hobbyists exchange messages and play at a distance can also cross boundaries that owners and institutions are only beginning to define. The episode is certain to sharpen calls for computer ethics, clearer rules, and better passwords.

stories.headline: Electronic Arts Puts Designers in the Spotlight
stories.dek: Computer Gaming World examines Trip Hawkins’ publishing model as Archon and Lode Runner command attention.
body: The October Computer Gaming World devotes a feature to Trip Hawkins and Electronic Arts, a publisher presenting software creators with the prominence usually reserved for recording artists. The approach arrives as computer games become more ambitious in design and presentation.

The same issue gives substantial attention to Archon: The Light and the Dark and features Lode Runner, alongside Combat Leader and The Cosmic Balance II. Together they show a market expanding beyond arcade imitation toward strategy, construction, and distinctive authorial voices.
